Lonely Planet writes that winter rain is "practically nil", whereas the Climi e Viaggi climate page makes December the wettest month, with 75 mm over 9 days (November 60 mm over 7 days, October 45 mm over 5). The same page gives average highs of 31 °C in July and 30 in August, and 20 °C in October. In short: summer is hot and busier, spring and autumn are good for walking, winter is quieter but you want a waterproof jacket.

Before you go: shoes, slopes and hours#

The lanes of the Civita, the Comune writes, can only be walked. Paving and steps are part of the route: shoes with a grippy sole, not sandals. Hours change with the season and we are now in autumn: the Casa Grotta, for example, from October to December opens Monday to Friday from 9:30 to 18:00, with last access at 17:40, and Saturday and Sunday until 19:00, with last access at 18:40.

Morning: Sasso Barisano and the Civita#

The Comune di Matera suggests a walking route that starts at the Villa Comunale and goes down via Pentasuglia to via D'Addozio, already inside Sasso Barisano. Here you meet the Monastery of Sant'Agostino, built in 1591 and partly rebuilt in 1747, whose church stands on the ruins of a rock-cut monastery; from the churchyard the view opens onto Murgia Timone and the Gravina canyon. A little further on, the church of San Pietro Barisano has an 18th-century facade over an underground church; according to the Comune's page, last updated in January 2024, the interior is not open to visitors.

From via Fiorentini you climb the Civita, the old heart dominated by the Cathedral. We did not verify the Cathedral's hours or admission: check on the spot.

Lunch break: what to taste#

Italia.it points to three dishes to start with: cialledda (bread soaked with tomato, garlic and olives, hot with egg and bay leaf or cold), Senise crusco peppers, and pignata, mutton slow-cooked in a clay pot with potatoes, tomatoes and soppressata. We name no restaurants because we have not verified any.

Early afternoon: Sasso Caveoso#

From the Civita you descend towards via Madonna delle Virtù, which runs along the edge of the ravine, to the rock-cut complex of Madonna delle Virtù and San Nicola dei Greci, founded between the 10th and 11th centuries, which hosts sculpture exhibitions from July to October. Then you reach Piazza San Pietro Caveoso, with the church rebuilt in 1706 and still used for worship, and Vico Solitario.

The Storica Casa Grotta di Vico Solitario is the clearest place to understand how people lived: the site gives admission at 8 € full and 5 € reduced, including the Neviera, a natural cave and the rock church of Sant'Agostino al Casalnuovo, plus a multilingual audio guide. The Ministry of Culture listing, updated in 2020 and with inconsistent hours on the same page, gives instead 3 € and 2 €: we would not use it as a reference. According to the ministerial entry, the house preserves the hearth, the bed, the stall with the mule's manger and the rainwater collection system, with its channelling and cistern.

End of the day: the viewpoints#

For the classic view of the stone nativity scene, Italia.it recommends the Belvedere of Murgia Timone in the Murgia Materana Park, especially towards evening. The Comune also mentions a Belvedere square reachable by car from the SS 7 Appia towards Laterza. Piazzetta Pascoli, in the centre, is a balcony over the Sassi without going far.

If you have a second day#

Three ideas with one certain fact each. The Crypt of Original Sin, which Italia.it lists among the rock churches not to be missed, dates from the Lombard period; it can only be visited by online booking, and in October the slots start at 9:30, 11:00, 12:30, 15:30 and 17:00, reduced to four (without the 17:00) from November to February. The ticket office is at the Azienda Agricola Dragone and you must arrive half an hour before. The Palombaro Lungo, under Piazza Vittorio Veneto, is a cistern dug in phases from the 16th century, 16 metres deep, 50 long and holding 5 million litres according to the official site; we did not verify hours and prices. Casa Noha, a short step from the Cathedral, is a project curated by FAI per Italia.it; we did not verify hours or prices.

How to order the day#

MorningSasso BarisanoFrom the Villa Comunale along via Pentasuglia and via D'Addozio, pausing at the churchyard of Sant'Agostino.

Late morningCivitaThe pedestrian lanes towards the centre and the Cathedral.

LunchA Matera dishCialledda, crusco peppers or pignata, per Italia.it.

Early afternoonSasso CaveosoMadonna delle Virtù, Piazza San Pietro Caveoso and the Casa Grotta, going in before 17:40.

Late afternoonViewpointMurgia Timone or Piazzetta Pascoli, in end-of-day light.

ConsiglioIn autumn the Casa Grotta closes at 18:00 on weekdays: put it before sunset and keep the viewpoints for later, when you no longer need tickets or hours.

How much it costs, on average#

The only cost we verified is admission to the Casa Grotta (8 €, an indicative average from the official site). For walking through the Sassi along the Comune's route we found no entry ticket on the pages we read. We read no prices for the Crypt, the Palombaro Lungo or the museums, so we do not quantify them. Meals and transport were not verified.

Common mistakes#

Turning up at the Crypt without a booking: it is online only.
Arriving at the last minute: you need to be there half an hour before the slot.
Trusting a single listing for Casa Grotta prices: three sources, three figures.
Climbing up and down without proper shoes.
Planning everything on summer hours in autumn.

What to skip#

With only half a day, skip the stops that require booking and keep the Comune's walk with a single visit, the Casa Grotta. The viewpoints cost nothing and remain the best moment.

More itineraries#

To try the same approach in other walking cities, read one day in Lecce or one day in Ortigia. If you are short of time and want a rain plan, there is what to do in Catania when it rains, and for thinking about how to build an itinerary with AI help, itineraries with artificial intelligence.

A route that adapts#

Matera is the kind of place where a wrong opening time or a missed booking wrecks the afternoon. It is the problem UNNIVAI wants to solve: a route of real places that adapts when the day changes. If you want to be among the first to try it, join the waitlist.

Verification note. Data read on 30 October 2026 on the pages listed in the sources: UNESCO, the Comune di Matera and its tourist portal MateraWelcome, Italia.it, the Casa Grotta website and the Ministry of Culture listing, the Crypt of Original Sin website, the Palombaro Lungo website, Lonely Planet Italia and a climate page. Where sources disagree (the Casa Grotta price, the date of the Sassi evacuation, winter rainfall) we say so. We did not verify the Cathedral's hours and admission, Crypt prices, Palombaro Lungo hours and prices, FAL train journey time and frequency, or where to eat. Prices as indicative averages: hours, closing days and bookings change, so always check official information before you set out.


# Palermo street food guide: markets, hours and what to order
URL: https://unnivai.com/en/blog/palermo-street-food-guide
Language: en
Updated: 2026-10-30

Palermo's three great markets look like three versions of the same place, but they keep three different clocks. The Capo and Ballarò are morning markets, the Vucciria is an evening place. Get the hour wrong and you find shutters down or an empty square, and Palermo becomes a hard city to read. This guide lines up the markets, says what to order, and where the sources disagree it says so.

In short. Go to the Capo and Ballarò in the morning, when the stalls are working and the fryers are on; leave the Vucciria for the evening. Order panelle and crocchè, an arancina, sfincione and, if you feel brave, pani ca meusa. About €10-15 per person (indicative, in cash) is enough to eat well. Avoid Sunday afternoon for the markets.

The Ballarò market in Palermo, between fruit and vegetable stalls and a steady flow of shoppers Photo: Benjamín Núñez González, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons
Early morningCapo marketEnter from Porta Carini and Via Cappuccinelle: panelle, sfincione, arancine, fruit and fish.

Late morningCathedral and AlbergheriaFrom the Capo you walk down to the Cathedral and then into the Ballarò district.

MiddayBallaròThe oldest and largest market: fried things, sfincione and the call of the vendors.

AfternoonA pastry shopA cannolo, ideally filled on the spot.

EveningVucciriaPiazza Caracciolo comes alive with the grills: stigghiola, pani ca meusa, a glass of something.

Which market to choose, and when?#

The Comune di Palermo tourism portal lists four names among the most important historic markets: Ballarò, the Vucciria, the Capo and Borgo Vecchio. It likens them to the souks of Muslim cities, with the vendors' call, the «abbanniata», as a soundtrack. For street food, though, the guides give each one a different role.

Palermo Food Tours, a tour operator whose text carries a check date of 25 October 2026, sums it up like this: the Capo and Ballarò are daytime markets, busiest from mid-morning and better on a weekday; the Vucciria is quietest by day and comes alive in the dark, when the grills come out. The Capo is in the Seralcadio district, near the Cathedral, and is, it says, one of the easiest to eat through, with panelle, sfincione, arancine and sweets next to fruit and fish. Ballarò, in the Albergheria, is the oldest and largest, and according to the same source the most local.

Keep in mind that «morning» does not mean «at dawn»: according to the Palermo Food Tours guide the two daytime markets are fullest between nine and one, when the fryers are going full. Saturday morning is the busiest time, with Palermitans doing their weekly shop.

Opening hours: where the sources disagree#

Be cautious here, because the written hours do not match.

Ballarò. According to the Comune it is open Monday to Saturday from 7:30 am to 8 pm, and on Sunday mostly in the morning only. Do Eat Better writes Monday to Saturday 7 am to 7 pm. The difference is half an hour in the morning and an hour in the evening.
Capo. The Comune says only «open every day in the morning and afternoon». Do Eat Better gives Monday to Saturday 9 am to 5 pm.
Vucciria. Here too the Comune writes «open every day in the morning and afternoon», but the guides say something else entirely: according to Do Eat Better by day it is nearly deserted and the real atmosphere begins after 9 pm, and Palermo Food Tours describes it as quiet by day and lively after sunset. It is probably the fruit and fish stalls that stay open in the morning while the street food moves to the evening; but that is our interpretation, not a data point.
Borgo Vecchio. Palermo Food Tours describes it as a market that wakes up in the late afternoon and evening, with grilled meat and stigghiola, mostly frequented by Palermitans.

One last warning: Palermo Food Tours writes that Sunday afternoon is the worst time for the markets, because many stalls close. The Comune confirms for Ballarò that Sunday is «mostly mornings only».

What to order: the classics in order of the day#

Panelle and crocchè. Panelle are chickpea-flour fritters, crocchè are potato and mint croquettes, and according to Do Eat Better they are eaten together in a sesame-seed roll, one of the most common naturally vegan street foods. The Comune lists them among the specialities sold at the Capo.

Sfincione. According to Towns of Italy it is a thick, soft focaccia with tomato, onion, anchovy, caciocavallo and breadcrumbs, sold by street vendors from big rectangular trays; Do Eat Better describes it as a rectangle of spongy dough and recommends it for breakfast at Ballarò. The Comune also mentions the «sfincionello».

Arancina. In Palermo it is feminine, and that is the rule on which Do Eat Better and Towns of Italy agree (for a comparison with Catania, see our guide what to eat in Catania, where it is masculine). The classic «al burro» has mozzarella and cooked ham; the «al ragù» has meat.

Pani ca meusa. It is the spleen sandwich. Towns of Italy describes it as veal spleen cooked in lard, served in a sesame bun with ricotta or caciocavallo; Do Eat Better speaks of spleen and lung in small pieces, boiled and fried in lard, and says you order it schiettu (lemon only) or maritatu (with cheese). That source gives about €3 at a Vucciria stall; Towns of Italy places the sandwich at the Vucciria or Ballarò.

Stigghiola and frittola. Stigghiola is lamb or veal intestine wrapped around a spring onion and grilled: Palermo Food Tours and Do Eat Better put it at the Vucciria, in the evening. Frittola is a mix of boiled and fried veal trimmings, sold from a covered basket: it is the one food on the route where Do Eat Better advises caution for sensitive stomachs.

Cannolo. Towns of Italy recommends asking for it «riempito al momento» (filled right now): in a serious pastry shop the shell and the ricotta stay separate until you order.

What it costs#

According to Do Eat Better most tastings cost between €1.50 and €5, and you can eat well for under €15 per person; for Ballarò it lists €1-5 per piece and for the Capo €2.50-6. For the same source a panelle and crocchè sandwich costs €2.50 at a place on the Capo. These are indicative figures, read on a single site: prices change. Palermo Food Tours and Do Eat Better agree on the practical point: bring cash and coins, because many stalls do not take cards.

How to put the day together#

Two sources suggest two different orders. Palermo Food Tours suggests starting early at the Capo, near Porta Carini, eating your way down through the fritters and sfincione, cutting across to the Cathedral and then entering Ballarò through the Albergheria: in about half a day you see two markets, the Cathedral and the Quattro Canti. Do Eat Better proposes the reverse order: Ballarò in the morning (8-12), the Capo at lunch (12-14) and the Vucciria from 9 pm.

We follow geography: the Capo and Ballarò are on the same line of walking between Via Beati Paoli and Via Vittorio Emanuele, as Palermo Mare Holidays also points out, and the Cathedral stands in between. But the order of the two markets matters less than the hour: be there before one.

ConsiglioDo not go to the Vucciria at 11 in the morning expecting the market you saw in the photos: Do Eat Better says so plainly and Palermo Food Tours confirms that by day it is the quietest. Keep it for the evening, even just for a drink in the square.

If you arrive out of hours#

If the markets are closed, the fry shops often are not. Palermo Mare Holidays (a page updated in March 2025, so worth re-checking) lists for instance a fry shop on Via Vittorio Emanuele open every day from 9 am to 1 am and one on Corso Camillo Finocchiaro Aprile open, it writes, 24 hours a day. These are not data dated to October 2026: call or check on a map before you set out.

Safety and manners#

Do Eat Better writes that the food is safe (high temperatures and a constant turnover of customers) and that the main risk is pickpocketing in the tightest parts of Ballarò: phone in a front pocket and bag closed. Palermo Food Tours gives the same advice for every crowded market. Another repeated rule: do not over-order at the first stall, and look for queues of locals.

What to leave out#

All three stops in the same morning: the Vucciria in the morning is the wrong choice.
Sunday afternoon: the stalls thin out.
A sit-down lunch: between tastings you already have a meal. Leave the table for the evening.

If you have another day#

To learn how to read a fish market, our guide to Catania's fish market has the same morning rhythm. In eastern Sicily, one day in Ortigia is another day to do on foot, and if it rains, what to do in Catania when it rains has indoor plans. If you wonder how to have an AI build a day like this without making up opening hours, read AI travel itineraries: what works.

If your day changes#

UNNIVAI rewrites the route when hours, rain or tiredness change: same markets, different order. If it sounds useful, join the first people in.

Information checked on 30 October 2026 on the sources listed. Hours and prices are read on operators' sites and guides and change during the year: check before you go. Where two sources disagree, we said so; venue names are quoted only as the sources report them.


# Milan in a weekend when it rains: a Plan B itinerary
URL: https://unnivai.com/en/blog/milan-in-a-weekend-in-the-rain
Language: en
Updated: 2026-10-30

Rain does not cancel Milan; it just reshuffles it. The centre is packed with museums, the metro reaches almost everywhere, and the big sights sit in two fairly compact areas. All you need is a sensible order and a few checks on hours and closing days, because that is where a wet weekend really goes wrong.

In short. On Saturday stay around Piazza Duomo: Museo del Novecento, the Cathedral and Duomo Museum, Galleria Vittorio Emanuele II. On Sunday move to the Castello Sforzesco and the Pinacoteca di Brera. On Mondays the main museums are closed, and The Last Supper must be booked weeks ahead: it is not a last-minute Plan B.

Piazza Duomo seen from above, the starting point of Saturday (a sunny day: in the rain it will look different) Photo: Elena Chochkova, CC BY-SA 3.0, Wikimedia Commons
How much does it actually rain in Milan?#

There is no "safe" month. According to the Italian Wikipedia entry on Milan's climate, average annual rainfall is about 920 mm over 82 days, with the peak in autumn, a secondary maximum in spring and a relative low in winter (around 40 mm in February). The same page notes that foggy days are becoming less frequent. These are climate averages, not a forecast: the practical point is that an October or November weekend in Milan can be dry or soaked, so have an indoor plan ready.

Rule one: one area per day#

The worst rainy-day route is one that crosses half the city at every stop. Here the advantage is clear: Saturday revolves around Piazza Duomo, where the Lombardia.info page puts Palazzo Reale about 120 metres from the Duomo and the Galleria Vittorio Emanuele II about 250. On Sunday you shift towards the Castello Sforzesco and Brera. We did not verify the walking distance between the Castello and Brera, so check the map before you leave.

Provalo
☔ Piove☀ Non piove

1. Duomo di Milano: Cathedral and MuseumAl coperto#

The single ticket for the Cathedral and the Duomo Museum, including the church of San Gottardo in Corte, costs 10 € full price and 5 € reduced, according to the official access page in force since 1 April 2025. On Wednesdays the Museum is closed and the ticket drops to 8 € and 4 €. On a weekend that does not affect you. The Duomo's hours are not straightforward: the ticket office in the Sala delle Colonne is listed as open 9:00 to 18:00, with the last ticket at 17:50, while another line on the same page mentions access through the north portal from 8:00 to 19:00 with last entry at 18:10. Lombardia.info gives 9:00-19:00. The sources do not match, so to be safe arrive before 17:50. There is a second discrepancy about the Duomo Museum: the official site says it is closed on Wednesday, while Lombardia.info says it is open Tuesday to Sunday and closed on Monday.

2. The Duomo terracesAll'aperto#

The terraces are the stop that suffers most in the rain. The official page mentions 135 spires, over 3,400 statues, a first level at about 31 metres and a central terrace at about 45, and says the mountains can be seen "on clear days". Official tickets for the terraces alone cost 18 € by lift and 16 € on foot (9 € and 8 € reduced). The Combo, which also includes the Cathedral and Museum, is 26 € by lift and 22 € on foot. We found no bad-weather closure rule on the pages we read: ask when you buy, or leave the climb for a clear day.

3. Galleria Vittorio Emanuele IIAl coperto#

According to the Lombardia Beni Culturali catalogue entry it is a "covered pedestrian street" with an iron-and-glass structure on a cross-shaped plan, designed by Giuseppe Mengoni. Work began in 1865 and the gallery opened two years later, still unfinished; the complex was completed about twelve years after that. At the centre of the octagon there is a mosaic of the House of Savoy coat of arms. It is the right place for the ten minutes between visits, when the rain eases for a moment and you want to stay dry. We do not name cafés or shops here: we did not verify any.

4. Museo del NovecentoAl coperto#

At Piazza Duomo 8, about 250 metres on foot from the Duomo stop on lines M1 and M3, according to the museum's site. Official hours: closed Monday, Tuesday to Sunday 10:00-19:30, Thursday until 22:30, last entry one hour before closing. We did not find ticket prices on the pages we opened, so we do not quote them. It is ideal for early Saturday because it does not force you to rush.

5. Castello Sforzesco: museums yes, courtyards noAl coperto#

The Castello museums are open Tuesday to Sunday, 10:00-17:30, with the ticket office closing at 16:30; the courtyards are free and open daily from 7:00 to 19:30, but they are outdoors. The ticket is valid for the whole day and covers all the museums. On the price the official page disagrees with itself: the body text says 10 € full and 5 € reduced, while the page description says 5 € and 3 €. Trust the body text, which is more detailed, and confirm at the ticket office. Every weekend at 11:00 there is a guided tour without booking, in English on Saturday and in Italian on Sunday, at 20 € with the museum ticket included. Entry is free for everyone on the first Sunday of the month.

6. Pinacoteca di BreraAl coperto#

Official hours: Tuesday to Sunday 8:30-19:15, last entry at 18:00, closed on Mondays. The "La Grande Brera" ticket costs 20 € full and 4 € for ages 18-25; it covers the picture gallery and Palazzo Citterio, which you can visit the same day and in the following six days. On the first Sunday of the month entry is free with compulsory booking. The 8:30 opening makes it a good way to start Sunday before the crowds.

7. The Last Supper: only if you have bookedAl coperto#

The Cenacolo Vinciano museum is open Tuesday to Sunday, 8:15 to 19:00 (last entry 18:45). The official site is blunt: booking is always compulsory, for everyone, even for free tickets. Sales open in three-month blocks, and the full ticket costs 15 €, 2 € for ages 18 to 25, free up to 18. The visit slot lasts 15 minutes and you must be at the ticket office at least 30 minutes before, or you lose your entry. If you do not already have a ticket, do not count on it as a Plan B.

How to order the weekend#

The real constraint is not the rain but the museum calendar. With these official hours, this order holds up best:

Saturday morningMuseo del NovecentoOpens at 10:00 and closes at 19:30, last entry one hour earlier. If you have a free evening, Thursday it stays open until 22:30.

Saturday middayGalleria Vittorio Emanuele IIA few minutes' walk away: a covered pause with no rush.

Saturday afternoonCathedral and Duomo MuseumGo in before 17:50. If the sky clears, consider the terraces.

Sunday morningPinacoteca di BreraFrom 8:30, last entry at 18:00: mornings are the calmest.

Sunday afternoonCastello SforzescoMuseums close at 17:30 and the ticket office at 16:30: arrive by 16:00.

OptionalThe Last SupperOnly with a booking already in hand, arriving 30 minutes before your slot.

ConsiglioBuy the Last Supper and Brera tickets online weeks ahead, and keep the Duomo for a moment when you already have a free hour: if the weather turns, your real Plan B is always the Museo del Novecento or the Castello.

Getting around in the rain: ATM#

According to ATM, the single 90-minute ticket costs 2.20 €, the daily ticket (24 hours from first validation) 7.60 € and the 3-day ticket 15.50 €. Two daily tickets come to 15.20 €, almost the price of a 3-day ticket, so for a weekend choose by how you move: the ATM page adds that you can pay with a contactless card and that from the fourth journey the system applies the daily fare. The Duomo stop is on lines M1 (red) and M3 (yellow). On which tram lines stop at the Duomo the sources disagree: Lombardia.info lists 2, 12, 14, 16 and 19, while the Museo del Novecento lists 2, 3, 12, 14, 15, 16 and 19. For the right tram, use the ATM app.

How much it costs, on average#

Adding up the official prices read on the pages, a weekend with the Duomo stairs Combo (22 €), the Castello (10 €) and Brera (20 €) costs about 52 € per person, or 67 € with the Last Supper. These are indicative averages, excluding the Museo del Novecento, whose price we did not verify, and excluding transport and meals. The Castello page also lists the YesMilano City Pass Standard at 60 € for 3 days, which includes transport, the Duomo with stairs, the Castello, the Museo del Novecento and other museums: do the sums for your own list, because it only pays off if you visit most of it.

Common mistakes#

Arriving on a Monday with a museum-only plan: the Castello, the Novecento, Brera and the Last Supper are all closed.
Assuming you can walk into the Last Supper without a booking.
Counting on the terraces under a grey sky.
Reaching the Castello at 17:00: the ticket office closed at 16:30.
Trusting a single site for the Duomo hours: as we saw, the sources do not agree.

What to skip#

With only one rainy day, skip the Castello and keep the Duomo, the Galleria and one museum between the Novecento and Brera. If you have not booked the Last Supper, do not waste time hunting for it: build the weekend without it.

If you have another day#

For the same plan-B thinking in another city, read what to do in Catania when it rains, or Rome in two days and Florence in 48 hours. To beat the worst of the queues anywhere, there is also Venice without the crowds, and for rebuilding an itinerary when the weather changes, how to use artificial intelligence for itineraries.

Plan B is built beforehand#

The problem with rain is not the rain: it is having to rebuild the programme from scratch, in the downpour, with your phone in your hand. It is the same problem UNNIVAI wants to solve: a route of real places that adapts when the day changes. If you want to be among the first to try it, join the waitlist.

Verification note. Data read on 30 October 2026 on the pages listed in the sources: the official websites of the Duomo di Milano, ATM, the Castello Sforzesco, the Museo del Novecento, the Pinacoteca di Brera and the Cenacolo Vinciano, plus Lombardia.info, the Lombardia Beni Culturali catalogue and Wikipedia. Where sources disagree (Duomo hours, the Duomo Museum closing day, the Castello price, tram lines) we say so. We did not verify prices or accessibility at the Museo del Novecento, nor the walking distances between the Castello and Brera. Prices as indicative averages: hours, closing days and bookings change, so always check official information before you set out.


# Cinque Terre on foot: trails, trains and what is closed
URL: https://unnivai.com/en/blog/cinque-terre-on-foot
Language: en
Updated: 2026-10-30

cinque-terre--al-via-i-lavori-nelle-stazioni-ferroviarie-d.html

UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Portovenere, Cinque Terre and the Islands::https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/826/
CinqueTerre.eu.com (private site), trail status (Italian)::https://www.cinqueterre.eu.com/it/cinque-terre-situazione-sentieri

--- The Cinque Terre are best walked with one question in mind: what is open today? Trail status here is not fixed. It moves with the weather, works and crowds, and the only page that counts is the park's. This article puts in order what we read on 30 October 2026 about trails, cards, trains and the Via dell'Amore, says where sources disagree, and leaves you a plan that survives a closure. UNESCO describes the landscape as a steep coast of about 15 km between Levanto and La Spezia, shaped over centuries by dry-stone terraces for vines and olives, which is why trails are maintained, and closed, by precise rules.

In short. On 30 October 2026 the park's map shows the Manarola-Corniglia stretch of the Blue Path as closed (skip it by train), while the Via dell'Amore is open only by reservation, one way (Riomaggiore towards Manarola) and from 9 am to 6 pm. To walk you need the Trekking Card (10 € adults, 15 € on high-attendance days) or the Train Card. From 14 November there are weekends with trains suspended for works: always check the official page before leaving.

Vernazza seen from above, from a viewpoint on the Blue Path Photo: СССР, CC BY-SA 2.5 ca, Wikimedia Commons
What is closed today?All'aperto#

The trail network has an official, updated page on the Cinque Terre National Park site, with a weather-alert message (when we opened it, it read "Nessuna allerta", no alert, dated 29 October 2026) and four route categories: tourist, hiking, expert and closed. The Blue Path, the coastal route linking the villages, appears like this: Riomaggiore-Manarola (the Via dell'Amore) as tourist, with a stated 25 minutes; Manarola-Corniglia as closed; Corniglia-Vernazza (1 h 30) and Vernazza-Monterosso (2 h) as routes for experts.

A useful cross-check: the private site CinqueTerre.eu.com lists the coastal Manarola-Corniglia stretch as closed "because of a landslide", but its page shows a last edit of 18 May 2026. The two sources agree on the closed stretch, but only the park's is current to the week we are writing. It is a good example of why you never copy a list of closures from a blog, this one included: we tell you how to read it, we do not promise it will be the same tomorrow.

The park itself warns that trails may be closed or limited for weather and safety, maintenance and crowd management, and adds that the card includes services and access but does not replace safety rules.

Which stretches can you actually walk?All'aperto#

With today's closures, the simplest route is a day in three pieces plus a train. Start in Riomaggiore and do the Via dell'Amore, which the park describes as one-way to Manarola, about 30 minutes. Then take the train from Manarola to Corniglia, because the walk between them shows as closed. From Corniglia walk to Vernazza (1 h 30) and, if you have the legs and the light, on to Monterosso (2 h). Adding the park's stated times gives about 4 hours of actual walking, stops excluded: that is our sum, not a park figure.

The 1.5 hours between Corniglia and Vernazza and the 2 hours between Vernazza and Monterosso are classed "expert" on the official map. The park's guidelines ask for closed shoes with a lugged, non-slip sole (open or smooth-soled footwear is banned, with fines) and remind you that walking in bad weather is prohibited.

MorningRiomaggiore, Via dell'AmoreEntry by reservation, one-way towards Manarola, about 30 minutes.

ThenTrain Manarola-CornigliaThe coastal path between them shows as closed: skip it by train, with the fare or card you chose.

MiddayCorniglia-VernazzaPark's stated time 1 h 30, route classed for experts.

AfternoonVernazza-MonterossoStated time 2 h. If the light fades, stop at Vernazza and take the train back.

EveningTrain backCheck the last train on Trenitalia before you set off. On regional trains leaving Levanto or La Spezia Centrale after 7:30 pm the evening fare applies, equal to band A.

How does the Via dell'Amore work?All'aperto#

It is the shortest and most regulated stretch. According to the official page, the entrance is in Riomaggiore, the route is one-way to Manarola, takes about 30 minutes, and individual visitors must reserve a time slot. Hours changed with the end of summer time: until 24 October 2026 it was open 9 am to 9 pm (last entry 8:30 pm); from 26 October 2026 to 28 March 2027 it is open 9 am to 6 pm with last entry at 5:30 pm.

Here the sources disagree on walking time: the trail map says 25 minutes, the access page says about 30, and the private site we cited says 900 metres and 20 minutes. It matters little, but do not time a train connection to the minute. The Via dell'Amore is included in both the Trekking Card and the Train Card: without a card you do not get in, and you book online on the card site or at park infopoints.

Which card do you need: Trekking, Train or single ticket?All'aperto#

It depends on how many times you board a train. The Trekking Card, per the park, includes the Blue Path between Monterosso, Vernazza and Corniglia, the Via dell'Amore, buses inside the villages, toilets in the stations (1 € for non-holders) and more. For an adult aged 12-69 it costs 10 € for one day, 17 € for two, 23.50 € for three; on high-attendance days that rises to 15, 26.70 and 37.50 €. The calendar of high-attendance days is a separate PDF on the park's site: we did not read it and do not give its dates.

The Train Card adds unlimited second-class travel on regional trains between Levanto and La Spezia. The price list changes on 2 November: until 1 November an adult pays 22, 29.50 or 35 € for one day depending on the band, while from 2 November to 31 December 2026 the park lists 17.30 € for one day, 29 € for two and 34 € for three. One discrepancy: Trenitalia lists the two-day card, band C, at 61.50 €, while the park's English page says 61.00 €. If you buy that band, check the amount at purchase.

A single regional ticket at the Cinque Terre fare costs, per Trenitalia, 5, 8 or 10 € depending on the day's band, until 1 November 2026; it must be validated and is valid 75 minutes for one direct trip. We did not read the fare in force after 1 November, so we do not state it. Finally, cards are non-refundable except in cases set by the rules (weather alerts, force majeure, a train strike for the train card), and two- or three-day cards are not refunded if even partly used.

Trains and works: when the line stopsAll'aperto#

After 1 November the picture changes, and it is worth checking before you book a room. RFI and the park report works on accessibility at Riomaggiore and Manarola stations (lifts and a new link at Manarola). To carry them out, trains will be suspended for 48 hours between Corniglia and La Spezia on the weekends of 14-15 November and 19-20 December 2026 and 9-10 January and 6-7 February 2027, and between Levanto and La Spezia from 10:30 pm to 6:30 am on Friday to Sunday nights of the same weekends. The site works every day, mostly at night.

For you this means two things. Riomaggiore and Manarola sit between La Spezia and Corniglia: on those weekends, for 48 hours, do not plan the Via dell'Amore around a train from La Spezia. And on the affected nights, decide before 10:30 pm how you get back after a long walk. The park refers readers to Trenitalia for updates.

How much to spend (indicative averages)#

A day on foot between the Via dell'Amore and the Blue Path, with an adult Trekking Card, costs 10 € (15 € on high-attendance days), plus the train tickets you use: between Manarola and Corniglia and back, on regional trains at the Cinque Terre fare, the range we read is 5-10 € a trip until 1 November. With a one-day Train Card from 2 November the park lists 17.30 € for an adult. These are indicative averages: they depend on the day's band, discounts and what is open.

What if the weather turns?Al coperto#

The park is blunt. With a yellow weather alert it advises against the trails and may stop selling the Trekking Card; with an orange or red alert it bans access to the whole network and suspends sales of all cards. On those days the plan becomes hopping between villages by train and strolling the old streets, no trails. The bus inside the villages is free with the card, but it does not link one village to another, and the card is not valid on La Spezia or Portovenere buses. For trail emergencies the guidelines give 112.

What to leave out#

Trying to do "the whole Blue Path" when a stretch is closed: two stretches done well beat an improvised detour.
City shoes: they are banned on the trails, and checks are not a detail.
A last-minute return: the Via dell'Amore closes at 6 pm with last entry 5:30 pm, and on works weekends the line can stop at night.
A calendar copied from a blog: trail status is read on the park's page, every time.

ConsiglioPut the stretch that depends on a reservation (the Via dell'Amore) and the ones that can close for weather (Corniglia-Vernazza and Vernazza-Monterosso) in the same day. In the morning open the park's page or stop at an infopoint, and if one of them drops out you still have a plan and the other. You gain peace of mind more than time.

If you have another day#

The Cinque Terre run on logistics and crowds: for another city where access and tickets matter, read Venice without the crowds, which uses the same checking approach. If you want an easier walking day, one day in Lecce is all flat. And if you wonder how to have an AI build an itinerary without inventing trail hours, see AI travel itineraries: what works.

If your day changes#

UNNIVAI is built to rewrite the route when an opening, the weather or tiredness changes: same walk, different order. If it sounds useful, join the first people in.

Trail status, hours, prices and works were checked on the official sources listed on 30 October 2026 and change often: check the park's page on the day. Where two sources disagree, we said so. We did not read the calendar of high-attendance days or the train fare after 1 November.


# Bologna in a day: tortellini, porticoes and a walking plan
URL: https://unnivai.com/en/blog/bologna-in-a-day
Language: en
Updated: 2026-10-30

Prenotazione-salita-alla-Torre-degli-Asinelli

Bologna Welcome, Clock Tower and Municipal Art Collections (Italian)::https://www.bolognawelcome.com/it/esperienze/300685/Visita-alla-Torre-dell-Orologio-e-alle-Collezioni-Comunali-d-Arte
Bologna Welcome, San Luca::https://www.bolognawelcome.com/en/blog/san-luca-eng
Basilica di San Petronio, info and hours (Italian)::https://www.basilicadisanpetronio.org/info-e-orari/
Basilica di San Petronio, visits (Italian)::https://www.basilicadisanpetronio.org/visite/
Musei di Bologna, Archiginnasio and Anatomical Theatre (Italian)::https://www.museidibologna.it/archiginnasio/
Dotta Confraternita del Tortellino, the deposited recipe (Italian)::https://www.confraternitadeltortellino.it/la-ricetta-depositata/
Bologna Welcome, ragù alla bolognese (Accademia Italiana della Cucina)::https://www.bolognawelcome.com/en/other/recipes-and-typical-products/ragu-alla-bolognese-2
Emilia Romagna Tourism, Quadrilatero del gusto (Italian)::https://emiliaromagnaturismo.it/it/itinerari/quadrilatero-del-gusto

--- Bologna is walked with a roof over your head. The porticoes work as a corridor between stops and, if the weather turns, the plan barely changes. This itinerary puts one walking day in order across square, towers, market and porticoes, with tortellini at the centre, and says where hours are seasonal, where sources disagree and what is closed right now.

In short. Morning around Piazza Maggiore, San Petronio (free entry) and the Clock Tower; lunch in the Quadrilatero; early afternoon at the Archiginnasio; if you have energy left, the San Luca portico. When we opened the official booking page, the Asinelli Tower was listed as closed for maintenance: the Clock Tower is the alternative it points to. The art collections are closed on Mondays.

A stretch of the San Luca portico, with arches climbing towards the sanctuary Photo: Puscas Vadim  (Nebbius), CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons
MorningPiazza Maggiore and San PetronioFree entry to the basilica, no reservation. The paid route through three chapels costs 5 €.

10:00 amClock TowerReservation required; from September to February the first entry is at 10:00 am.

LunchQuadrilateroVia Clavature, Drapperie, Pescherie Vecchie: cured meats, fresh pasta and stalls to eat at.

AfternoonArchiginnasio and Anatomical TheatreThe old university seat: audioguide visit, entries every 10 minutes.

LateSan Luca porticoOptional, uphill: more than 2 km of slope or steps.

Provalo
☔ Piove☀ Non piove

What is closed or changes in autumn?All'aperto#

Three things to know before you go. First, the Asinelli Tower. Bologna Welcome's booking page carried the notice "Torre Asinelli chiusa per manutenzione nell'area", with a pointer to the Clock Tower. When it reopens, the climb needs a reservation, has 498 steps and no lift. Second, the Clock Tower has seasonal hours. From 7 September 2026 to 28 February 2027 the first entry is at 10:00 am and the last at 6:20 pm, with three entries an hour. Third, the Municipal Art Collections in the same palace have different hours (Tuesday and Thursday 2-7 pm, Wednesday and Friday 10 am-7 pm, Saturday, Sunday and holidays 10 am-6:30 pm) and are closed on non-holiday Mondays.

The practical consequence is simple: if Monday is all you have, the tower works but the collections do not, and the Asinelli needs checking. If you have a choice, pick a Tuesday to Friday.

Morning: Piazza Maggiore and San PetronioAll'aperto#

Start in the square where everything converges. The Basilica of San Petronio, according to its official site, has free entry and needs no reservation for individual visits. To enter the chapels of the Magi (Bolognini), San Sebastiano and San Vincenzo Ferrer you buy the paid route on the spot: 5 € full and 3 € reduced, from 10:00 am to 5:30 pm with last entry at 5:15 pm. Other single chapels and the Presbytery are visited only on request by email, at least a week ahead, at 3 € per person for each.

We do not give the nave's visiting hours: services change them, and the basilica's site warns of days when guided visits are cancelled for events. Check the page on the day.

Clock Tower and Palazzo d'AccursioAl coperto#

It is the alternative climb to the Asinelli, and in autumn it is convenient because it opens at 10:00 am. The ticket includes the audioguide visit of the tower (about 40 minutes) and entry to the Municipal Art Collections (about an hour): 10 € full, 7 € reduced, according to Bologna Welcome. Reservation is mandatory, you show up 5 minutes before and if you are late you cannot go up on the next slot. The meeting point is the Sala Farnese, on the second floor of Palazzo d'Accursio, Piazza Maggiore 6. The summit terrace is reached by a narrow stair, with a waiver signed on site and a ban under 8 years of age; there is no lift.

Lunch in the Quadrilatero: where tortellini liveAll'aperto#

The Quadrilatero is the centre's shop-and-market district: according to Emilia Romagna Tourism its perimeter is drawn by the crossing of via Rizzoli, via dell'Archiginnasio, via Farini and via Castiglione. On via Clavature there is one entrance of the Mercato di Mezzo, with stalls to eat from, take away or at shared tables; on via Capraie and via Drapperie you find delis and shops with mortadella, fresh pasta and sweets; on via Pescherie Vecchie, tigelle and cured meats for an aperitivo. The same source names the Osteria del Sole, in Vicolo dei Ranocchi, described as the oldest osteria in Bologna, where only wine is served and everyone brings their own food.

We do not name tortellini restaurants, because we read none on the sources we consulted. What we can give you is a yardstick: the Dotta Confraternita del Tortellino reports the deposit of 15 April 2008 at the Chamber of Commerce, which defines the classic shape, the filling, the thickness of the pasta and a final weight of 5 grams, with the pasta cut into squares 3 cm on a side. According to the same page, for about a thousand tortellini you need 10 eggs and a kilo of flour for the pasta; 300 g of pork loin, 300 g of raw ham, 300 g of mortadella, 450 g of Parmigiano Reggiano and 3 eggs for the filling; and for the broth a kilo of beef, half a hen, celery, carrot, onion and salt. Asking whether the broth is made in-house and whether the pasta is rolled daily is a more useful test than any ranking.

For ragù the source is Bologna Welcome, which gives the updated version deposited by the Accademia Italiana della Cucina at the Chamber of Commerce (the original dates from 1982): 300 g of minced beef (diaphragm, belly or shoulder), 150 g of pancetta, 50 g each of carrot, celery and onion, 300 g of tomato passata or peeled tomatoes, half a glass each of dry white wine and whole milk, broth, and about two hours of cooking.

Early afternoon: Archiginnasio and Anatomical TheatreAl coperto#

The Archiginnasio, the old university seat, is visited with an audioguide or a guided tour. According to the Musei di Bologna page, updated in July 2025 and so worth rechecking, audioguide visits run Monday to Saturday from 10:00 am to 5:40 pm, with entries every 10 minutes and a duration of 40 minutes; the full ticket is 10 € and the reduced 8 €. Guided tours cost 12 € full and leave at fixed times (for July and August, in Italian at 1:30 and 3:30 pm). Put this stop after lunch: it is entirely indoors and takes no more than an hour.

The porticoes and the San Luca porticoAl coperto#

The porticoes are not a backdrop: UNESCO inscribes them as a serial site of 12 portico ensembles, and the Comune notes that the whole network is 62 km long. The listing dates from 28 July 2021. Among the twelve ensembles is "San Luca".

The San Luca portico links the city to the sanctuary. Here the sources disagree: the Comune speaks of about 3,600 metres and notes that the traditional count of 666 arches is actually slightly lower, depending on how they are counted; Bologna Welcome gives 3.5 km and 666 arches. On the route the Comune is precise: from the Arco Bonaccorsi you follow via Saragozza, flat, for about a kilometre and a half; then for more than 2 kilometres you climb, partly on steps. Bologna Welcome says to continue under the portico from Porta Saragozza. The alternative, per Bologna Welcome: bus 20 to the church of San Martino in Casalecchio di Reno, then bus 58 to the sanctuary. We did not read walking times: our estimate is no less than a couple of hours there and back on foot, and it is only an estimate.

How much to spend (indicative averages)#

With the figures read: Clock Tower with collections 10 €, Archiginnasio with audioguide 10 €, San Petronio's paid route 5 €. In all about 25 € in tickets for one adult, with San Luca and the basilica free. These are indicative averages: they depend on discounts, days and cards such as the Bologna Welcome Card (which the sources list as free for the Asinelli and the Clock Tower).

What to leave out#

Too many towers: if the Asinelli is closed, the Clock Tower is enough for a panorama.
Mondays for museums: the art collections stay closed.
San Luca in the rain or at day's end if you are tired: it is uphill and best in full daylight.
The hunt for the "right" restaurant: the broth test and a Quadrilatero stall are better.

ConsiglioBook the Clock Tower for 10:00 am and do San Petronio right after: they are a few steps apart, the first runs on fixed slots and the second does not. That way you reach the Quadrilatero at lunchtime, and the Archiginnasio, with entries every 10 minutes, fits wherever it falls.

If you have another day#

After Bologna the logic changes but the yardstick stays: Florence in 48 hours for another walkable historic centre, with reservations to make ahead. If the food is what won you over, what to eat in Catania is the southern answer, with the same care for sources. And to learn how to have an AI build a day like this without inventing opening hours, read AI travel itineraries: what works.

If your day changes#

UNNIVAI is built to rewrite the route when an opening, the weather or tiredness changes: same walk, different order. If it sounds useful, join the first people in.

Hours, prices and opening days were read and checked on the official sources listed on 30 October 2026 and change during the year: check before you go. Where two sources disagree, we said so. We did not verify San Petronio's nave hours or walking times to San Luca.


# What to eat in Catania: 10 tastes in order of the day
URL: https://unnivai.com/en/blog/what-to-eat-in-catania
Language: en
Updated: 2026-10-29

Eating in Catania is not solved with a restaurant: it is solved with a well-built day. You start with a granita, pass through the market, have something fried for lunch and finish with a pasta that here has an opera-house name. This guide puts the tastings in the order that makes sense, tells you when to order them, what they cost on average and what is better left alone.

In short. Morning: granita and brioche. Mid-morning: fish market and street food. Lunch: arancino and pasta alla Norma. Afternoon: sweets. Evening: horse meat or fish, if you like. Indicative average prices: €18-33 for a day of tastings, dinner at a restaurant excluded.

MorningGranita with briocheAlmond, pistachio, coffee or lemon, with Sicilian brioche. About €4.

Mid-morningFish market and surroundingsWatch the market and taste standing up.

LunchArancino and pasta alla NormaIn Catania the fried one is masculine; Norma is the first course not to skip.

AfternoonCannolo and sweetsSheep's ricotta and marzipan.

EveningHorse meat or fishOne choice, not both.

1. Granita and brioche#

The Catanese breakfast is granita (water, sugar and fruit) with a Sicilian brioche, leavened with eggs and scented with vanilla or citrus. The flavours to start from are almond, pistachio, coffee and lemon. Travel365 recommends trying almond first; for coffee, the same source suggests having it with brioche and whipped cream. If you are short on time, pick just one flavour and do not argue with the menu. Indicative average cost: about €4.

2. Seltz with lemon and salt#

At the city's kiosks they drink a seltz made with lemon juice, sparkling water, salt and a pinch of bicarbonate. It sounds odd until it is hot. About €2: Do Eat Better Experience quotes €1.50-2 and says to drink it right away while it is still foaming, because waiting flattens the fizz.

3. The fish market and its street food#

The fish market, which locals call "a piscaria", is a few steps from Piazza Duomo, near the Fountain of the Seven Channels. You do not have to buy anything: just walking through it is a taste of the city. Around it you find kiosks and small places selling food to eat standing up. According to Do Eat Better Experience, the closest street food is the paper cone of fried fish at Scirocco Sicilian Fish Lab (€9, with a long queue around lunchtime); Travel365 gives an average of €7 per person for the same place. The two sources do not agree, so treat €7-9 as a range. For hours, practical tips and what to avoid, read the guide to the Catania fish market: hours and how to visit.

4. Arancino (masculine)#

In Catania it is arancino, and it has the cone shape that recalls Etna: rice with ragù, breaded and fried. It costs around €2 in bars and simple rosticcerie. If you want a serious comparison, taste the classic ragù one before trying variations. Travel365 mentions Pasticceria Savia on Via Umberto (with a queue) and Munnu Arancinu on Via Lavandaie (sweet versions too): we have not tried them or checked their hours.

5. Pasta alla Norma#

Pasta with tomato sauce, fried aubergine, salted ricotta and basil. The name recalls Bellini's Norma; he was born in Catania. It is the first course that best represents the city. In simple trattorie it costs around €8; in smarter places it goes up.

6. Spaghetti alla carrettiera#

Oil, raw garlic, pepper and grated pecorino, with some variants adding tomato. The name comes from the cart drivers, who travelled for long stretches and wanted a quick pasta made with ingredients that keep well. It is the right choice if you have already had the Norma and want a second pasta, drier. About €8 according to Travel365.

7. Horse meat#

It is a true Catanese speciality, not a curiosity for tourists: meatballs, sausages and steaks. The best-known street to try it is Via del Plebiscito. As a main course you spend from about €10. Travel365 also lists the Polpetteria on Via Santa Filomena (average €20 per person) and Trattoria da Mario on Via Crociferi (fixed menu around €20). If it is not for you, there is no obligation.

8. Swordfish#

Usually grilled with a drizzle of oil. It is the dish to order if you want fish in the evening, from about €15 as a main course. Always ask what is fresh that day. Travel365 notes that in June, in nearby Acitrezza, there is a festival dedicated to swordfish.

9. Cannolo#

A crisp shell with sheep's ricotta cream. The practical advice is to eat it filled to order: a cannolo that has been filled for hours loses its crunch, which is half the pleasure. About €2 in bars.

10. Sant'Agata sweets#

The minnuzze di Sant'Agata are small cassatine with sponge cake, ricotta, marzipan and a candied cherry, always with white icing. The olivette are almond-paste sweets shaped like olives and coloured green: Travel365 puts them at about €20 a kilo. According to the same source the patron saint is celebrated from 3 to 5 February and during those days the sweets are everywhere; outside January and February, ask before you walk across town looking for them.

ConsiglioDo not do it all in one day. Pick four tastings and walk between them: in Catania the centre is compact and walking is easy.

Seasons: what to eat and when#

Not everything is there all year. Sicilian Red Orange PGI (Tarocco, Moro and Sanguinello) is hand-picked and, per the product specification reported by Qualigeo, is on the market from December to May: Tarocco from December to May, Moro between December and March, Sanguinello between February and April. If you visit Catania at the end of October, as we are right now, it is not yet its season. Bronte green pistachio PDO, on the other hand, is harvested by hand every two years, in the odd-numbered ones, says the protection consortium: 2026 is an even year, the next harvest is in 2027. For pistachio ice cream and granita the rule is the label: if the PDO matters to you, ask.

How much to spend on a day of tastings#

The figures are Travel365 average prices and the total is our own estimate. Granita with brioche €4, seltz €2, arancino €2, pasta alla Norma €8, cannolo €2: €18 in total. Add a horse meat main course (from €10) or a swordfish one (from €15) and you land between €28 and €33. For a restaurant dinner, Travel365 gives averages between €12 and €35 per person in the places it lists. Carry coins and small notes: Do Eat Better Experience warns that many market stalls will not change a €20 or €50 note for a purchase of a few euros.

How to order without awkwardness#

One rule works almost everywhere: do not touch displayed food with bare hands, point at what you want and let the person behind the counter handle it (Do Eat Better Experience gives this rule for the market, but it is good manners in a rosticceria too). If there is a queue, hold your place: in Catania the line is fluid and anyone who leaves a gap risks being overtaken. On meal times, Travel365 explains that people eat late: going out after 8 pm is normal, kitchens stay open until 10 pm and many restaurants close around 11:30 pm or midnight. Book if you have a specific place in mind.

Vegetarian and gluten-free#

By ingredients, pasta alla Norma contains no meat; the classic arancino does, because it is filled with ragù. Granita and cannolo are counter sweets, but the brioche and the shell contain gluten. Travel365 flags four addresses for specific needs: Easy Bistrot Glutenfree in Piazza Carlo Alberto (100% gluten-free, average €15), Occhio al Glutine on Viale Mario Rapisardi (gluten-free bakery, average €8), Cuore Fresco near Piazza Duomo (healthy cooking and vegan dishes, average €15) and PLANTE Lab on Via Sant'Anna (plant-based, average €18). We have not visited them: phone or write first, especially if you have coeliac disease.

What to avoid and what NOT to do#

Do not have breakfast, lunch and dinner in the same place. Catania is eaten on the move.
Do not order a coffee right after fried fish. Do Eat Better Experience recommends the seltz, which cleans the palate.
Do not trust multilingual photo menus outside the main squares: the same source calls them tourist traps.
Do not hunt for Sant'Agata sweets out of season as if they were always on sale.
Do not buy raw fish to carry around if you have no fridge: in the heat it is a risk.

Getting there#

If you land in Catania, the AMTS Alibus line links the airport with the city: according to the airport website it leaves the terminal between 04:40 and 00:30, roughly every 25 minutes. The ticket costs €4 and is valid for 90 minutes on the other AMT urban lines too, whereas tickets for the other lines are not valid on the Alibus. From there the centre is walkable.

How to organise it#

If it rains, the bar and rosticceria stops work anyway: see the plan in what to do in Catania when it rains. The fish market, however, is largely open-air, so in the rain bring closed shoes and a plan B for lunch. If you have the evening free, plan where to have dinner first: the good places fill up fast. If you have another day in the area, see one day in Ortigia.

If the day changes#

UNNIVAI rewrites the route when weather, time or hunger change. If you need it, be among the first.

Verification note. Prices and hours are indicative averages from the sources listed (Travel365, the Bronte Green Pistachio PDO Consortium, Qualigeo, Do Eat Better Experience, Siviaggia, the airport website and AMTS) and change during the year: check before you go. Checked on 29 October 2026. We have not personally verified the individual venues mentioned.


# Venice without the crowds: when to go and where to eat
URL: https://unnivai.com/en/blog/venice-without-the-crowds
Language: en
Updated: 2026-10-29

Venice is not a city to "do": it is a city to cross in a certain order, at certain hours. The problem is not the city, it is the moment you arrive. This guide puts together what the official pages of the City and of AVM say (access fee, vaporetto, rules of conduct) with what tourism sites say about hours, quieter districts and bacari, flagging every time where sources disagree. Most of the sources are in Italian, so the names of pages and terms are given as they appear.

In short. Today there is no access fee to enter Venice (the 2026 trial ended on 26 July; in 2027 it returns on fixed days between March and August, from 8:30 to 16:30). To avoid the crowds go early in the morning or after sunset, put the middle of the day in Cannaregio and Castello, and eat at the counter in a bacaro rather than at the tables around San Marco. For vaporetto and markets always check the official pages: prices and days change.

Early morningRialto: market and ErbariaThe market gives its best in the first part of the morning; fruit and vegetables, according to two sites, close at 13:30.

Mid-morningCannaregioFondamenta, canals and the ghetto: here the city runs at the pace of its residents.

LunchA bacaroCicchetti standing at the counter, an ombra of wine and off you go: the Venetian lunch is short.

Early afternoonCastelloThe least touristy district according to local sites: Via Garibaldi, the gardens and the Arsenale.

AfternoonVaporetto to the GiudeccaA single long ride, to look at the city from the water.

EveningCannaregio or DorsoduroAfter sunset many day visitors have already left.

Do I have to pay to enter Venice?#

The access fee is the most frequent question, and it is also where the sources contradict each other. The City of Venice's information page, updated on 13 March 2026, still describes the 2026 calendar: from 3 April to 26 July, for 60 non-consecutive days. The official fee site (cda.ve.it), on the other hand, states at the top that the 2026 trial has ended and that from 27 July 2026 the fee does not apply: you can visit Venice without any payment or request for exemption. This second statement is the most recent, and it matches today's date: no fee to pay.

For the future, the same site lists the 2027 days: March 26, 27, 28, 29; April 2, 3, 4, 9, 10, 11, 16, 17, 18 and 23 to 30; May 1, 2, 7, 8, 9, 14, 15, 16, 21, 22, 23 and 28 to 31; June 1 to 6, 11, 12, 13, 18, 19, 20, 25, 26, 27; July 2, 3, 4, 9, 10, 11, 16, 17, 18, 23, 24, 25, 30, 31; August 1, 6, 7, 8, 13, 14, 15. The time band is 8:30 to 16:30. Procedures and amount for 2027 are not published: the site says they will be announced by 31 December and that the 2027 FAQ are not yet available. From the City's page, which refers to 2026, the fee applied to people over 14 visiting the old city, and those excluded or exempt included residents of the municipality of Venice, workers and students, people staying overnight in accommodation within the municipality (who must still register on the portal) and residents of the Veneto region. The penalty for not paying was 25 to 150 euros (plus the fee). These are 2026 rules: check them again before a trip in 2027.

How do you avoid the crowds in practice?#

The simplest strategy is also the oldest one: change the hour. A local guide read for this article lists early morning as the quietest time, when canals and lanes are still empty, and the evening after sunset, when many day visitors have left; it adds that the low season, from November to February excluding holiday periods, is a good time for a calmer Venice. The same logic appears in the City of Venice's guidance, which among its 12 good practices asks visitors to "plan the trip on days of lower traffic" and to stay more than one day to get to know the lesser-known places too.

The second lever is the district. Local sites point to Cannaregio and Castello as the most authentic sestieri: in Cannaregio the church of Madonna dell'Orto (where Tintoretto's tomb is) and the Misericordia canal, in Castello Via Garibaldi, the gardens and the Arsenale. Among lesser-known places the same guide cites the cloisters of the Carmelitani Scalzi and of San Francesco della Vigna. Among the official Venezia Unica itineraries there is one on the Giudecca and San Giorgio Maggiore that ends with the view from the San Giorgio bell tower, 75 metres tall, and one on Cannaregio. Keep in mind that the more commercial tourism sites also carry paid offers: I used only the descriptive information, not the purchase suggestions.

Vaporetto: which ticket do you really need?#

On the official AVM site the main prices are these: ordinary 75-minute ticket on the single network 9.50 €, 24 hours 25 €, 48 hours 35 €, 72 hours 45 €, 7 days 65 €. The time ticket is valid on all land and water vehicles and allows unlimited trips within the time band that starts at first validation; connections to Marco Polo airport are not included. The ticket must be validated as soon as you board, by touching it to the validator, and each change of vehicle needs a new validation. The page also lists a "Rolling Venice - Youth" offer with a 72-hour ticket at 27 €: I did not read the conditions, so check before relying on it.

A calculation that helps: two 75-minute tickets cost 19 €, less than the 24-hour ticket (25 €); three tickets cost 28.50 €, more than the 24-hour one. So the 24-hour ticket only pays if you expect at least three trips at different times of the day. These are sums on today's indicative prices and depend on how you use the lines; in Venice many stretches are done on foot anyway.

How should you behave?#

The City of Venice runs a campaign, "Enjoy Respect Venezia", with 12 concrete gestures. Some apply to everyone: walk on the right and in single file in narrow lanes, do not stop on bridges, do not lead bicycles even by hand; do not use church steps, wells, quays and monuments as picnic areas (for eating there are the public gardens); around Piazza San Marco you may not stop outside the designated spaces to eat or drink; camping or bivouacking, walking about shirtless, diving or swimming are not allowed; do not feed the pigeons and do not leave padlocks. These are the rules that make the difference between a good day and a fine, and between being a guest and being a weight on the city.

Where to eat for real: the bacaro#

The bacaro is Venice's typical tavern: small, rustic, often wooden, with the cicchetti displayed in a case near the counter. According to the Visit Venezia site (which notes commercial partnerships in its text) the most common cicchetti are sarde in saor (sweet-and-sour sardines), baccalà mantecato (whipped salt cod), meatballs, mozzarelle in carrozza, fried fish and tramezzini, and they go with an ombra of wine or a spritz. The round from bacaro to bacaro is done at lunchtime or at aperitivo time; the same source notes that many tourists take a tray of cicchetti as a full meal, and that this misses the point of the ritual, which is a roaming tasting.

How much does it cost? The site gives 0.60 to 2 € for a glass of wine and 1 to 3 € for a cicchetto. The page is undated, so treat it as an order of magnitude, not a price list. For areas, it cites Cannaregio (along the Fondamenta degli Ormesini), Santa Croce, Dorsoduro (Campo Santa Margherita) and Castello, described as the least touristy sestiere and therefore rich in bacari frequented by locals. I am not giving you the name of a specific place: I have not verified it on an official page and bacari change management and hours. The practical criterion is different: choose where you see people chatting at the counter, not where a waiter hands you a menu in the street.

Rialto market: when to go#

At Rialto you find the historic market, with the fish market and the Erbaria area. Two Venetian accommodations that describe the market on their sites give hours that are nearly identical but not the same: the fish market Tuesday to Saturday (7:30 to 12:00) for one, Tuesday to Friday (7:30 to 12:00) for the other; fruit and vegetables Monday to Saturday until 13:30 for both. Saturday is therefore the uncertain day: I found no City page resolving the discrepancy. One of the two sites also recalls that the fish market's Loggia dates from 1907, the work of Domenico Rupolo, with different capitals inspired by fishing, and that the island of Sant'Erasmo is traditionally tied to the produce sold here. If you want to see the market at its best, go in the first part of the morning: it is the moment when daily life is most visible. Later, the stalls empty out.

What to leave out#

Piazza San Marco at peak hour: look at it at the start or end of the day and give the middle of the day to something else.
The seated meal at the most photographed spots: move two or three lanes away and look for the counter with people standing.
The idea of doing everything in one day: Venice rewards those who stay longer and do not chase lists.

If you have more days#

For another art city organised by day read Florence in 48 hours without pointless queues; for a walking itinerary in a southern city there is One day in Lecce on foot; for another iconic city ordered by area, Rome in two days, and for food in order of the day What to eat in Catania.

A plan for your day#

Choosing the right hour, district and ticket depends on the day you arrive, the weather and the rules in force at that moment: it is exactly the kind of decision UNNIVAI wants to make automatic. Join the waitlist.

Checked on 29 October 2026 on pages opened for this article. Hours, prices and access rules change during the year: check the official sources before you go.


# One day in Lecce: baroque, pasticciotto and walking lanes
URL: https://unnivai.com/en/blog/one-day-in-lecce
Language: en
Updated: 2026-10-29

Lecce is a city to walk with your chin up. Lecce baroque does not come across in a photo: it needs a slow pace, pale stone that changes colour with the light, and a sweet stop or two. This itinerary puts one walking day in order, with few stops and the reason for each, and says plainly where hours change with the season.

In short. Breakfast with a pasticciotto, the amphitheatre in Piazza Sant'Oronzo and the Faggiano museum in the morning, the castle around midday, the baroque route (Duomo, Santa Croce) in the afternoon. From October to March the churches close at 6 pm and the amphitheatre at about 3:30 pm, so the order of the stops matters. Avoid Mondays.

BreakfastPasticciotto in a café in the centrePastry and custard, even better lukewarm. It is the Salento morning ritual.

9:30 amRoman amphitheatrePiazza Sant'Oronzo: in autumn and winter it opens early and closes early, so it goes first.

10:45 amFaggiano museumOpen every day until 8 pm: the wildcard stop. Entry around 5 €.

12:30 pmCharles V CastleEntry only on a guided tour of about 50 minutes, at fixed times.

LunchInner streetsA simple Salento dish, away from the main squares.

2:30 pmDuomo, Santa Croce and churchesSingle ticket: get in by 5:45 pm, because everything closes at 6.

Provalo
☔ Piove☀ Non piove

Before you go: days and hours to checkAll'aperto#

You can see Lecce in a day only if the opening hours line up, and in autumn they do not line up on their own. The churches on the baroque route are open every day from 9 am to 9 pm according to the official site, but between October and March they close at 6 pm, with entry allowed until 15 minutes before. The amphitheatre, on the Ministry of Culture site, is listed as closed on Monday and open 9 am to 3:30 pm on winter hours; the online ticket office, when consulted, showed 9 am to 3 pm for ticket sales and 9 am to 3:30 pm for the public. The castle is open Tuesday to Sunday.

The practical consequence is simple: whatever closes early (the amphitheatre, the castle tour) goes in the morning, whatever stays open until evening (the churches, the Faggiano museum) goes in the afternoon. If Monday is the only day you have, drop the amphitheatre and the castle and keep the baroque route and the Faggiano.

Morning: breakfast with a pasticciottoAll'aperto#

Start where locals start. A pasticciotto is a shell of shortcrust pastry filled with custard and baked; it is recognised as a traditional agri-food product of Puglia and, according to the Italian Wikipedia entry, people in the Salento habitually have it for breakfast in local cafés and pastry shops. People argue about whether it should be eaten hot: some want it straight from the oven, but the same source points out that a good handmade pasticciotto can be enjoyed at room temperature too.

One story not to take as gospel: the tale that it was born by accident in 1745 in Galatina at the Ascalone bakery is a legend told in several versions, and the article that launched it, from 2005, cannot be verified. The oldest document known for the name of the shape, a 1707 inventory in Nardò, only mentions copper moulds. If someone tells you the date as a fact, smile and order.

We do not name places: in a city with this many pastry shops, walk into one where the counter is full and people are eating standing up.

The Roman amphitheatre in Piazza Sant'OronzoAll'aperto#

It is the first surprise of the day: at the most central point of the city, below the level of the square, there is a Roman amphitheatre. According to the Ministry of Culture it measured about 102 by 82 metres and could hold between 12,000 and 14,000 people; it was brought to light from 1900 by the archaeologist Cosimo De Giorgi, and today about a third of it can be seen, while the rest lies under the square and the surrounding buildings.

Here the sources do not agree, and it is worth knowing. The Ministry site and the official ticket office list a full ticket at 5 € (reduced 2 €), while the tourism portal Visit Lecce says 10 € for adults. We suggest trusting the official ticket office and checking at the moment of purchase. The ticket office also states that entry is free on 4 November 2026 and on the first Sunday of each month, and that the Roman Theatre is temporarily closed for refitting works. The Roman Theatre Museum, on the Comune's page, is listed as open Monday to Saturday from 9:30 am to 1 pm, with afternoon visits by reservation only. Dates and works change: check first.

Faggiano museum: the indoor breatherAl coperto#

The Faggiano museum is open every day from 9:30 am to 8 pm and costs 5 € for single visitors, with discounts for young people (free from 0 to 8 years, 3 € from 8 to 16, according to the site). Of the museums on this route it has the most convenient schedule: it stays open until 8 pm, so it works as a wildcard. We put it in mid-morning because it is small and does not force any awkward scheduling; if the weather turns, you can move it a few hours either way and lose nothing.

Charles V Castle: the one stop with a fixed timeAl coperto#

The castle can only be visited with a guide, in turns of about 50 minutes. From October to May, Tuesday to Sunday, tours leave at 10:30, 11:30 and 12:30 and then at 4, 5, 6 and 7 pm. The guided tour costs 10 € full and 6 € reduced and can be bought online on the site, which also lists exhibitions with a separate ticket. We suggest the 12:30 tour: it does not clash with anything else and leaves lunch right after. If you turn up without booking, go to the ticket office a few minutes before departure, as the site advises.

Afternoon: Piazza del Duomo, Santa Croce and the single ticketAl coperto#

The heart of Lecce baroque is done with one ticket: the Duomo with its crypt, the Basilica of Santa Croce, the churches of San Matteo and Santa Chiara, the old Seminary with its cloister and the Museum of Sacred Art. The official site lists 11 € full, 5 € reduced and 24 € family; if you also want the view from the Duomo bell tower, the full ticket costs 21 € (13 € reduced, 48 € family), with climbs every 20 minutes. The ticket office is at Piazza Duomo 5.

Give the façade of Santa Croce some time before going in: it is where the stone says the most. And do not make the mistake of leaving the churches for last at 5:50 pm: with closing at 6 and entry allowed until 15 minutes before, you risk paying for a ticket and seeing little.

How much to spend (indicative averages)#

Adding up the figures read on the official sites: amphitheatre 5 €, Faggiano museum 5 €, baroque route 11 €, castle 10 €. That is about 31 € in tickets for one adult, about 41 € if you add the Duomo bell tower. These are indicative averages and depend on reductions, free days and temporary exhibitions: they are not a promise.

Plan B: if the weather changes#

In the rain the plan rewrites itself naturally. The amphitheatre and the square take a quarter of an hour even under clouds; the rest is almost all indoors. Put the Faggiano and the castle in the worst hours and leave the churches for a clear spell. In the widget above you can try the swap.

What to leave out#

Too many museums: with the amphitheatre, the Faggiano and the castle you already have three indoor visits. One fewer is fine if you want to walk.
Lunch on the main square: two blocks from the most photographed squares are enough to change quality and prices.
The 5:50 pm rush: the churches deserve calm.

ConsiglioIf Monday is all you have, flip the idea: keep the Faggiano museum and the baroque route, leave the amphitheatre and the castle for another day. And if you can choose, on 4 November 2026 entry to the amphitheatre is listed as free.

If you have another day#

After Lecce, baroque Sicily is a different breath: see one day in Ortigia for a walking itinerary with the same logic, or what to eat in Catania if food is what won you over. If you wonder how to have an AI build a day like this without making up opening hours, read AI travel itineraries: what works.

If your day changes#

UNNIVAI is built to rewrite the route when weather, hours or tiredness change: same walk, different order. If it sounds useful, join the first people in.

Hours, prices and opening days were read and checked on the official sources listed on 29 October 2026 and change during the year: check before you go. Where two sources disagree, we said so.


# Florence in 48 hours without pointless queues
URL: https://unnivai.com/en/blog/florence-in-48-hours
Language: en
Updated: 2026-10-29

Florence goes wrong in two ways: standing in line in the sun outside a museum, or running back and forth because you never looked at the calendar. In 48 hours you can avoid both if you think about three things: which days are closed, what has to be booked at a fixed time, and what you can leave open. This itinerary puts the Duomo and the Accademia on the first day and the Uffizi on the second.

In short. Day 1: the Brunelleschi Dome (at a booked time), the Duomo and the Galleria dell'Accademia. Day 2: the Uffizi, ideally with a ticket already bought, then Florence on foot. Never on a Monday: the Uffizi and the Accademia are closed. Check strike notices and free days.

Day 1 · morningBrunelleschi DomeTime fixed at purchase, 5 minutes' tolerance, ID required. There are 463 steps.

Day 1 · late morningCathedral and Piazza del DuomoThe Cathedral is free; the other monuments need the Pass.

Day 1 · afternoonGalleria dell'AccademiaThe David and more. Open until 6:50 pm, but ticket sales stop 30 minutes earlier.

Day 2 · morningUffiziNamed ticket, best bought in advance. Open from 8:15 am.

Day 2 · afternoonFlorence on footNo tickets: the rest is a stroll.

Quale giorno ti serve?
EntrambiGiorno 1Giorno 2

Day 1: Duomo, Dome and Accademia#

You start where the Pass forces you to be on time: the Dome. The Brunelleschi Pass includes entry to the Baptistery of San Giovanni, Giotto's Bell Tower, the Dome, the Museo dell'Opera del Duomo and the basilica of Santa Reparata, with one entry per monument, valid for 3 calendar days. Validity starts from the date chosen for the Dome, and the booked day and time cannot be changed: choose carefully. The other monuments can be visited with no time restriction.

On the Dome, the official site is clear: the climb takes about 45 minutes, there are 463 steps and no lift, it is not recommended for people with heart problems, vertigo or claustrophobia, and since 1 March 2025 you must show an ID document with your ticket. Backpacks and medium or large bags go in the cloakroom before entering, and the entrance is the Porta della Mandorla, on the north side of the Cathedral. The site allows at most 5 minutes early or late compared with the time you chose.

After the Dome, the Cathedral is free to enter and needs no Pass. A few things to know, all from the Opera's official site: the Museo dell'Opera del Duomo is closed on the first Tuesday of each month for maintenance, and the mosaics of the Baptistery vault are not visible because they are being restored. If the Baptistery is your reason to buy the Pass, keep that in mind.

The afternoon is for the Galleria dell'Accademia. According to the museum's site it is open from 8:15 am to 6:50 pm with last entry at 6:10 pm, but ticket sales close 30 minutes before closing time: arrive with some margin. The full ticket is 20 €, the reduced one 2 € for young people aged 18 to 25, and booking costs 4 € if you do it by phone with Firenze Musei. The Accademia "strongly" recommends booking, because without a reservation waiting times can be long. On 4 November 2026 and every first Sunday of the month entry is free, but on those days the booking service is not active and you wait your turn at the door.

Day 2: Uffizi and Florence on foot#

The Uffizi are open Tuesday to Sunday from 8:15 am to 6:30 pm, last entry 5:30 pm. The ticket is named, and the price changes with the day of purchase: 25 € full if bought on the same day, 29 € if bought earlier. There is also an "Afternoon" promotion, since 1 January 2026: for those who enter from 4 pm onwards the ticket costs 16 € (20 € if bought in advance). The museum occupies the first and second floors of the building put up between 1560 and 1580 to a design by Giorgio Vasari, and the names the site mentions include Giotto, Botticelli, Leonardo, Raphael, Michelangelo and Caravaggio.
